title: Japan's 3D Secure Mandate: What the First Year of Data Shows About Fraud and Approvals
summary: Japan's 3DS mandate cut stolen-card fraud but doubled ATO and dropped completion rates 19 points. A look at what the first year of data actually shows.
body_markdown:
## The Objection: "3DS Is Mandatory, So Why Anything Else?"


Japan made 3D Secure (3DS) mandatory for card-not-present transactions in April 2025. One year later, the merchants seeing the best approval rates aren't the ones sending every transaction through authentication. According to Forter, they're the ones routing roughly 2% of traffic through 3DS, after their own risk models have already sorted clear fraud from clear legitimate buyers.


Forter reports that transactions without 3DS complete at roughly 94%, while transactions routed through 3DS in the first six months of the mandate completed at roughly 75%. That 19-point gap is not a rounding error. It's nearly $1 of every $5 customers try to spend.


3DS is the compliance floor. It is not, by itself, a fraud strategy or an approval-rate strategy. The merchants closing the gap use it selectively, not universally.


## Mandatory Doesn't Mean Every Transaction Gets 3DS


As described in secondary sources citing JCA Guideline v6.0, p.38, the Japan Consumer Credit Association (JCA, 日本クレジット協会) Credit Card Security Guideline outlines three operational patterns for how merchants apply 3DS:


-


**Pattern 3 (パターン3):** 3DS on all transactions.


-


**Pattern 2 (パターン2):** 3DS at card registration, with merchant discretion at the point of payment.


-


**Pattern 1 (パターン1):** Merchant discretion at both card registration and payment.


The difference matters. A merchant on Pattern 2 or Pattern 1 can let low-risk transactions skip the 3DS challenge entirely, provided they meet the associated security requirements. A merchant that defaults to Pattern 3 applies maximum friction to every buyer.


Recurring charges follow a separate rule: 3DS applies at signup, not on every monthly rebill. Merchant-initiated transactions, mail/telephone orders, and certain wallet-based payments (Apple Pay, Google Pay) fall outside the mandate's scope, as documented in Stripe's Japan exemptions guide.


The JCA also set a target of 80% of EC cardholders enrolled in 3DS by the end of March 2025. Whether that target has been fully met remains unconfirmed in published data.


The takeaway: the mandate created a framework with meaningful flexibility. Merchants who treat it as "3DS on everything" are choosing the most restrictive interpretation, not following a requirement.


## What Happened After the Mandate: The Data


The mandate did what it was designed to do for stolen-card fraud. Forter's data shows stolen credit card fraud's share of total fraud risk dropped roughly 40% between May and November 2025 and held at that lower level. Stripe reports dispute rates across its Japan network fell more than 30% year over year.


Adyen observed a similar pattern: a gross success rate decline of roughly 1.6 percentage points across its Japan merchants, with the net success rate dropping about 0.8 points after retries. These are meaningful gains. 3DS works for the problem it was built to address.


But fraud pressure didn't disappear. It moved.


Account takeover attacks doubled by October 2025 compared to pre-mandate levels and have stayed elevated. Forter describes this as the balloon effect: squeeze one fraud vector and the pressure shifts to another.


A DGBT survey from October 2026 found that 68.2% of EC operators did not experience a decrease in fraud incidents after the mandate took effect. For 32.7% of respondents, fraud actually increased.


The most commonly reported fraud type, at 32.4%, was card spoofing that bypasses 3DS entirely.


It is worth noting that Forter, DGBT, Cacco, and Akuru (ASUKA) are fraud-prevention vendors or conducted vendor-sponsored surveys. Their data is cited here with that context.


The costs also show up in less obvious places. The Cacco EC survey found that 49.5% of EC operators received card-company fee-increase requests in 2025, nearly double the 27.6% reported in 2024. Akuru's CEO describes what he calls "invisible revenue loss": chargeback liability shifted away from merchants after the mandate, so direct fraud losses dropped from view. But issuers tightened approval rates for merchants with higher fraud exposure, and that tightening erodes revenue without generating any alert or notification.


Consider a mid-size EC merchant processing JPY 500 million annually. If issuer-side tightening reduces their approval rate by even 2 percentage points, that's JPY 10 million in revenue that simply vanishes.


No chargeback report flags it. No fraud dashboard shows it. It looks like customers who didn't buy.


### The Stripe Counterpoint


Stripe's Japan network data tells a more encouraging story on the surface: 60% of 3DS-routed transactions passed without a challenge step, with an average 93% conversion rate. Those are real numbers from a large network.


But Stripe itself notes the figures are averages across its platform over a limited timeframe. Initial pockets of lower authentication success required direct collaboration with issuers and AI-driven calibration of data fields per issuer preference.


Averages conceal the range. A major Japanese tax-donation marketplace that applied 3DS to all transactions after the mandate saw its payment success rate drop by roughly 17-18%, according to Forter. That's a concrete example of what a 93% average doesn't capture: individual merchants, especially those in categories with unusual transaction patterns, can experience far worse outcomes.


## The Real Question: Minimize 3DS Triggers While Maximizing Approvals


Issuer behavior varies more than most merchants realize. Akuru reports some merchants saw challenge rates near 50%, despite card companies suggesting 20% was typical. Without per-issuer data for your own traffic, you can't tell where friction sits or which issuers are costing you revenue.


Stripe's experience reinforces this. Even with strong headline numbers, reaching those numbers required issuer-specific optimization: adapting data fields and authentication flows per issuer. Protocol compliance alone does not produce good outcomes. Per-issuer calibration does.


There's also a structural trap for merchants who let fraud accumulate. Under the mandate framework, merchants who exceed JPY 500,000 in fraud chargebacks for three consecutive months are classified as "fraud-exposed." That designation limits their exemption flexibility and triggers additional authentication requirements at the worst possible time. The threshold is low enough to catch mid-size merchants during seasonal spikes.


Japan's card fraud rate across all channels sits at about 0.03% (JCA data, Q2 2026, covering 48 major operators and excluding foreign-issued cards). That blended rate includes in-store transactions and understates EC-specific risk. When the underlying fraud rate is this low, even modest over-blocking destroys more revenue than the fraud it prevents. That's Corgi Labs' argument, and the math supports it: for most EC merchants, false declines cost significantly more than actual fraud losses.


## How Pre-Authorization ML Complements 3DS


The pattern that produces the best results is straightforward. Place machine-learning risk scoring upstream of 3DS, before the authentication decision:


1.


**Decline clear fraud pre-authorization** so it never reaches 3DS. Issuers see cleaner traffic from your merchant account, which supports higher approval rates over time.


2.


**Let clearly legitimate customers through without 3DS** where an exemption applies to the merchant. These buyers complete their purchase without the friction of a challenge step.


3.


**Route only borderline transactions to 3DS.** For these cases, 3DS adds a legitimacy signal and shifts chargeback liability. This is where authentication adds value rather than friction.


This approach also covers the gaps 3DS can't reach. Account takeover, which doubled post-mandate, happens before the payment step and operates outside 3DS's scope. Non-3DS payment flows, including merchant-initiated transactions and certain wallet payments, bypass authentication entirely. Pre-authorization scoring trained on your transaction data addresses both.


The revenue case extends beyond fraud prevention. False declines, where legitimate buyers are blocked, are invisible to most merchants because no chargeback is generated and no alert fires. Pre-authorization models trained on merchant-specific data recover these transactions by scoring buyer intent against your own patterns, not network-wide averages.


The difference between a 75% completion rate on 3DS-routed transactions and a 94% completion rate on transactions not sent through 3DS isn't just a Forter statistic. It's the revenue you recover when your risk model is precise enough to keep most of your traffic out of the authentication flow entirely.


For background on Japan's fraud landscape and why low chargeback rates mask real losses, see our earlier analysis:[Japan's Hidden Fraud Crisis](https://www.corgilabs.ai/insights/japan-fraud-hidden-crisis) . For a broader look at how 3DS performance varies across regulated markets,[3DS Success Rates by Country](https://www.corgilabs.ai/insights/3ds-strategies-by-market) covers the data market by market.


## What Comes Next


3DS is here to stay in Japan. The question isn't whether to comply. It's how little authentication friction you can apply while staying compliant and keeping fraud below threshold.


The merchants gaining ground are the ones who know, per issuer and per transaction type, where 3DS helps and where it costs them. If you don't have that visibility yet, start there.
